Pregnancy

When Can You Feel Your Baby Move? Quickening Explained

Updated: August 5, 2026

Written and edited by Mohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama — checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Most people can feel their baby move for the first time between 16 and 25 weeks of pregnancy, and in a first pregnancy it is often closer to 20 to 25 weeks. Those first movements are called quickening, and they usually feel like flutters, bubbles, or light taps rather than clear kicks. An anterior placenta or a busy day can make them harder to notice, so a quiet start is normal. This guide covers when movement usually starts, what it feels like, and the one change that always deserves a same-day call.

Most people feel movement between 16 and 25 weeks

For most pregnancies, the first noticeable movements arrive somewhere between 16 and 25 weeks. If this is your first baby, expect the later end of that range: many first-time parents feel nothing until 20 weeks or beyond, and that is completely normal. In second and later pregnancies, people often recognize movement earlier, sometimes around 16 weeks, simply because they know what they are feeling. Your baby has actually been moving since the first trimester. Ultrasounds show stretches, rolls, and kicks long before you can sense any of it. The window is about when the movements become strong enough, and you become still enough, for the two to finally meet.

If you are 18 or 20 weeks along and have felt nothing, try not to read too much into it. Quiet weeks at this stage are common, especially in a first pregnancy or with an anterior placenta. Mention it at your next routine visit so your team can listen to the heartbeat and check the placenta's position. If you have reached about 24 weeks without ever feeling movement, call your midwife or doctor rather than waiting for the next appointment. That call is standard practice, not an overreaction, and most of the time it ends with reassurance and a clear picture of what has been muffling the signal.

What quickening actually feels like

Quickening is the old word for the first movements you can feel, and the sensations are famously easy to miss. Parents describe flutters, bubbles popping, popcorn, a small fish turning over, or a light tap from the inside. Early on it can be almost impossible to tell apart from gas or a rumbling stomach, which is why many people only recognize it in hindsight. You are most likely to notice it while lying down quietly, especially on your side, or sitting still after a meal. Movement is easier to feel low in the belly at this stage because your uterus has not yet risen far above your pubic bone.

Over the following weeks the sensations change character. Flutters turn into distinct pokes, then into rolls, stretches, jabs, and proper kicks you could not mistake for digestion. Many babies are most active in the evening, when you finally sit down, or after you eat, though every baby has its own habits. In these early weeks there is nothing you need to count or record. Enjoy the novelty, tell people or keep it private, and let the movements build on their own schedule. Formal attention to patterns comes later in pregnancy, once movement is strong and frequent enough to have a rhythm worth knowing.

Why an anterior placenta delays the feeling

An anterior placenta sits on the front wall of your uterus, between the baby and your belly. It is a normal place for a placenta to attach and it does not harm the baby or the pregnancy. It does act like a cushion, so early movements are absorbed before they reach your skin. People with an anterior placenta often feel first movements later in the 16 to 25 week window, feel them more softly, and notice them at the sides and low in the belly rather than front and center. Your ultrasound report or your care team can tell you where your placenta sits.

The placenta is not the only variable. A baby who faces inward kicks toward your spine, busy days drown out subtle sensations, and body shape and abdominal muscle tone change what reaches the surface. Each pregnancy is different too, so feeling movement at 17 weeks last time and nothing at 19 weeks this time does not signal a problem by itself. One thing an anterior placenta does not change: later in pregnancy, once your baby has an established pattern, you should still feel regular movement every day. If the cushion ever seems to explain away a real slowdown, treat it as a slowdown and call.

When movement becomes regular, and when others can feel it

Somewhere between about 24 and 28 weeks, movement usually stops being an occasional surprise and becomes part of daily life. Your baby develops sleep and wake cycles, often 20 to 40 minutes at a time, and you start to learn a personal rhythm: active after breakfast, quiet mid-afternoon, lively at bedtime. There is no set number of kicks that fits every baby, so the useful knowledge is what normal looks like for yours. It can help to note the date of those first flutters and anything that seems to wake your baby up in BeMama or a notebook, so you have a rough timeline to look back on.

Partners usually have to wait a few weeks longer than you do. Kicks strong enough to feel from the outside typically arrive in the late second trimester, often between about 24 and 28 weeks, and an anterior placenta can push that later still. To improve the odds, pick a quiet evening when the baby is already active, have your partner rest a warm hand low on your belly, and wait without pressing or chasing the movement. It often takes several tries. A partner who feels nothing for a while is not missing a problem; from the outside, timing and luck matter as much as strength.

A decrease in movement deserves a same-day call

Once your baby has an established pattern, usually by around 28 weeks, one rule matters more than any tip in this article: if you notice a clear decrease or a significant change in that pattern, contact your maternity care team the same day. Do not wait until morning, until the next appointment, or until you are sure. Care teams expect these calls, they take them seriously, and they would rather check ten times than miss once. Reduced movement is one of the few warning signs that only you can notice, which is exactly why the standard advice everywhere is to report it promptly.

If you are unsure, lie on your side somewhere quiet and pay attention to your baby for a stretch of time. If movement still seems reduced, call. Do not use a home Doppler, a snack, or a cold drink as a substitute for that call: hearing a heartbeat does not rule out a problem, and there is no strong evidence that food or drink reliably wakes a baby who needs checking. The same rule applies every time it happens, even if a previous check was fine. This article is general education; your midwife or doctor knows your pregnancy and is always the right place to take a concern.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Fetal movement patterns become meaningful after movement is established, but there is no single pattern that fits every pregnancy. A prenatal professional may recommend a specific movement-counting method based on the situation.

A noticeable reduction or change from the baby’s usual activity deserves prompt contact with maternity care. A completed count or app total cannot prove fetal wellbeing.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can time and record movement observations exactly as your care team instructs. Do not repeat counts for hours or wait for the app to reassure you when movement is reduced.

When to seek help

Contact your maternity unit immediately for less movement than usual or the threshold provided by your care team.

Sources and further reading

  • ACOG — Special Tests for Monitoring Fetal Well-Being
  • CDC — Urgent Maternal Warning Signs and Symptoms

Links lead directly to guidance from the organizations named above.

Key takeaways

  • Most people feel the first movements between 16 and 25 weeks, often later in a first pregnancy.
  • Quickening feels like flutters, bubbles, or light taps and is easy to mistake for gas at first.
  • An anterior placenta cushions early movements, so noticing them later and more softly is normal.
  • Partners can often feel kicks from the outside between about 24 and 28 weeks.
  • A noticeable decrease in an established movement pattern deserves a same-day call to your care team.

Frequently asked questions

What does baby movement feel like at first?

Early baby movement usually feels like flutters, bubbles, gentle taps, or a light rolling sensation low in the belly. Many people mistake it for gas until it repeats in the same spot over several days. As the weeks pass, the flutters grow into unmistakable pokes, rolls, and kicks.

What is quickening in pregnancy?

Quickening is the traditional term for the first fetal movements a pregnant person can feel, usually between 16 and 25 weeks. It marks when movement becomes noticeable, not when it begins, since babies move from the first trimester. The exact timing varies with placenta position, body type, and whether this is a first pregnancy.

Does an anterior placenta affect baby movement?

An anterior placenta does not reduce your baby's movement, but it can muffle how much of it you feel. First movements often arrive later in the usual window and feel softer, especially at the front of the belly. Once a daily pattern is established you should still feel it, and any clear decrease still deserves a same-day call.

When can my partner feel the baby kick?

Most partners can feel kicks from the outside in the late second trimester, often between about 24 and 28 weeks. That is usually a few weeks after you first feel movement on the inside. An anterior placenta or an inward-facing baby can add more waiting time, and a quiet evening with a still, patient hand improves the odds.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
